title: The Island That Sank in a Night

pages.text: In the school library, Seyram found a book with a glowing island on its cover. “Atlantis,” she read. “A great island city that sank beneath the sea.” Her classmate Yaro laughed. “Is it real?” “Let us ask Mr Ayitey,” she said.
sentences: In the school library, Seyram found a book with a glowing island on its cover.
“Atlantis,” she read.
“A great island city that sank beneath the sea.” Her classmate Yaro laughed.
“Is it real?” “Let us ask Mr Ayitey,” she said.
pages.alt: Two students hold a book with an island on its cover in a school library.

pages.text: Mr Ayitey placed a globe on the desk. “The first writer to tell us about Atlantis was a Greek thinker named Plato, more than 2,300 years ago. He wrote about it in two books, Timaeus and Critias. We know of it from Plato, so the first question is: what did he actually say?”
sentences: Mr Ayitey placed a globe on the desk.
“The first writer to tell us about Atlantis was a Greek thinker named Plato, more than 2,300 years ago.
He wrote about it in two books, Timaeus and Critias.
We know of it from Plato, so the first question is: what did he actually say?”
pages.alt: A teacher stands by a globe with an old Greek scroll drawing beside it.

pages.text: “Plato said the island lay beyond the Pillars of Hercules, which means the Strait of Gibraltar,” said Mr Ayitey. “He wrote that it was huge, larger than Libya and Asia put together. Its rulers grew powerful and tried to conquer lands around the Mediterranean, but Athens stopped them.”
sentences: “Plato said the island lay beyond the Pillars of Hercules, which means the Strait of Gibraltar,” said Mr Ayitey.
“He wrote that it was huge, larger than Libya and Asia put together.
Its rulers grew powerful and tried to conquer lands around the Mediterranean, but Athens stopped them.”
pages.alt: A map shows the Strait of Gibraltar with a large island drawn beyond it.

pages.text: “Then,” said Mr Ayitey, “Plato wrote that earthquakes and floods came. In a single unbearable day and night, the island sank beneath the sea.” Yaro’s eyes went wide. “A whole city, gone in a night?” “That is what Plato wrote,” said Mr Ayitey. “Notice the words: what Plato wrote.”

“Notice the words: what Plato wrote.”
pages.alt: A shining island city sinks into dark waves as lightning flashes.

pages.text: “So why is it a mystery?” asked Seyram. “Because nobody has found it,” said Mr Ayitey. “There is no archaeological evidence of Atlantis. And scholars disagree about what Plato meant. Some think he invented the story as a lesson about greed and power. Others think it may echo a real disaster.”

“There is no archaeological evidence of Atlantis.
And scholars disagree about what Plato meant.
Some think he invented the story as a lesson about greed and power.
Others think it may echo a real disaster.”
pages.alt: A teacher lists two ideas on the board: invented story, memory of real event.

pages.text: “Which real disaster?” asked Yaro. “One idea is the great volcanic eruption on the island of Thera, today called Santorini, around 3,500 years ago. It devastated cultures in the Aegean Sea. But Thera does not match Plato’s island in size or place, so many experts remain unconvinced.” Yaro wrote: not a perfect match.

pages.alt: A volcano erupting over a small Mediterranean island, with a question mark.

pages.text: “What would count as proof?” asked Seyram. “Ruins, with datable remains, in the right place, matching Plato’s description,” said Mr Ayitey. “Lots of people have claimed to find Atlantis in many places. So far none of those claims has convinced the experts.” Yaro smiled. “So the evidence is… still missing.”

pages.alt: Students examine maps with many different Xs marked for Atlantis and all crossed out.

pages.text: At the end, Seyram wrote: Atlantis is Plato’s story. We do not know if it was real, invented or a memory of a disaster. “And that,” said Mr Ayitey, “is an honest answer. Real cities have vanished beneath the sea or into the sand, but Atlantis, as Plato described it, has never been found.” The end.
